source_says: Mooney estimated “there must have been 7,000 Comanche about 1690”
source: Mooney (1928), as given in Swanton, Indian Tribes of North America, p. 314

source_says: Knife River villages: “the Big Hidatsa village was established around 1600”; Awatixa Xi’e the oldest of the three
source: Wikipedia, “Knife River Indian Villages National Historic Site” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Northern Arapaho tradition (1892) of the Kiowa at the Three Forks of the Missouri, applied to the Plains Apache only on the assumption that they were already with the Kiowa (kept off the division track)
source: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), pp. 155–56

source_says: Northern Arapaho tradition (1892): when they first knew the Kiowa, the Kiowa “lived about the Three forks of the Missouri”; date ours (“probably about or before 1700”)
source: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), pp. 155–56

source_says: Opler: “a judicious estimate of all Lipan Apache in 1700, including those living in Mexico, would be about 6,000”
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Opler, “Lipan Apache”, p. 945

source_says: The great Dakota village of Kathio (Izatys) at Mille Lacs, the source of the Rum River; Du Lhut counted “40 Sioux villages in the vicinity” in 1679
source: Wikipedia, “Battle of Kathio” (site coordinates and participants) (belligerent: Mdewakanton Dakota)

source_says: “In 1700 they were, according to Le Sueur, on Blue Earth River near the Iowa”
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: Winter 1700–01: 60 lodges of Wahpekute Santee winter at Le Sueur’s Fort L’Huillier
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 726

source_says: Winter 1700–01: 150 lodges of Yankton winter with Le Sueur at Fort L’Huillier on the Blue Earth River; in May 1701, 200 lodges camp near the fort
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 726

source_says: 1701: the Iowa join the tribes gathering at Fort L’Huillier on the Blue Earth River, then flee west again
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Wedel, “Iowa”, p. 434

source_says: Le Sueur, 1702: the Sioux number 4,000 families
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 748

source_says: Iberville, 1702: 1,500
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Bailey and Young, “Kansa”, p. 472, table 2

source_says: Iberville (1702): 2,000 “Panas” families, “a population in excess of 10,000, assuming a minimum of five individuals in a family” (Parks)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, p. 563

source_says: Ulibarrí, leaving Taos on 20 July 1706, meets “several friendly Apache bands, probably Jicarilla” on “the upper courses of the Canadian and Cimarron rivers” (identification probable; centre ours)
source: Wikipedia, “Juan de Ulibarrí” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Ulibarrí at El Cuartelejo, “the main village… on Ladder Creek”, 1706; at least five Cuartelejo rancherías
source: Wikipedia, “El Cuartelejo” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: After leaving Fort L’Huillier the Iowa “may have chosen to live along the Little Sioux River below Spirit and Okoboji lakes” (date ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Wedel, “Iowa”, p. 434

source_says: Lehmer: of more than 60 Arikara village sites, perhaps 22 occupied at once, at 40 houses and 10 to a household: 8,800 for the early 18th century
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Lehmer, “Plains Village Tradition: Postcontact”, pp. 246–48, table 1

source_says: Lehmer: villages provisionally Hidatsa, about 1675–1750, hold over 640 houses; at Thompson’s 13 to a household, “over 8,300”
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Lehmer, “Plains Village Tradition: Postcontact”, pp. 246–48, table 1

source_says: Lehmer: six sites between Square Buttes and the Heart River, about 1675–1750, with some 620 houses: a Mandan population “of over 8,000”
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Lehmer, “Plains Village Tradition: Postcontact”, pp. 246–48, table 1

source_says: Bourgmont: three Arikara villages on the west bank of the Missouri above the Niobrara, and 40 villages farther upriver on both banks (kept off the division track)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Arikara”, p. 366

source_says: Bourgmont lives at “the Missouria village at the mouth of the Grand River”, from 1712
source: Wikipedia, “Étienne de Veniard, Sieur de Bourgmont” (site coordinates and participants); Wikipedia, “Fort Orleans” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Bourgmont, about 1714: the Otoe at a village on Salt Creek about 10 leagues from the mouth of the Platte; no Otoe villages east of the Missouri after this
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Schweitzer, “Otoe and Missouria”, p. 447

source_says: Before about 1730 the Jicarilla and Carlana, “close relatives” of the Cuartelejo and Paloma, “lived in fixed villages along the foothills of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains” (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Gunnerson, “Plains Village Tradition: Western Periphery”, p. 244

source_says: Vermale’s map of 1717 shows 10 Padouca villages north of the Pawnee villages; earlier maps had put the Plains Apacheans south of the Pawnee (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Foster and McCollough, “Plains Apache”, p. 928

source_says: Lehmer: “a conservative estimate for the year 1719 is 15,000, based on historical sources” (the Wichita “and closely related groups”)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Lehmer, “Plains Village Tradition: Postcontact”, p. 247

source_says: Lasley Vore site on the Arkansas in Tulsa County: “a Wichita village of about 6,000 people, as described by… La Harpe” in 1719
source: Wikipedia, “Lasley Vore Site” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Du Tisné finds “two likely Taovaya villages… near the present-day Neodesha, Kansas”, 1719
source: Wikipedia, “Taovaya” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Du Tisné’s two Taovaya villages near Neodesha, 130 grass houses and 200–250 warriors each: between them 2,080–2,600 people (the Taovaya only; a partial count)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Newcomb, “Wichita”, pp. 550, 561

source_says: The Villasur expedition passes through El Cuartelejo, 1720
source: Wikipedia, “El Cuartelejo” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Pawnee and Otoe attack Villasur’s camp just south of the Loup–Platte confluence near Columbus, 14 Aug. 1720
source: Wikipedia, “Villasur expedition” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Pawnee and Otoe attack Villasur’s camp at the Loup–Platte confluence, 14 Aug. 1720 (the Loup villages were the Skiri’s; division ours)
source: Wikipedia, “Villasur expedition” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Renaudière: a Pawnee village of 150 lodges 15 leagues up the Loup, and eight more villages farther upriver about half a league apart
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, pp. 517–18

source_says: Fort Orleans built beside the Missouria village near the mouth of the Grand River, Nov. 1723
source: Wikipedia, “Fort Orleans” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Bourgmont reaches “the main Kaw village on the Missouri near Doniphan” on 8 July 1724: “a large settlement, with at least 1,500 persons”
source: Wikipedia, “Étienne de Veniard, Sieur de Bourgmont” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: July 1724: Bourgmont finds the principal Kansa village on the west bank of the Missouri north of Independence Creek, Doniphan County
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Bailey and Young, “Kansa”, pp. 462–63

source_says: Bourgmont reaches the Padouca (Apache) village on the upper Little Arkansas, probably near Lyons, 18 Oct. 1724: 140 dwellings, “about 800 men, more than 1,500 women, and about 2,000 children”; the chief claimed twelve villages
source: Wikipedia, “Étienne de Veniard, Sieur de Bourgmont” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Saukamappee’s youth (about 1730): “a large camp of the Snake Indians on the Plains of the Eagle Hill”; date from his age, place from Thompson’s gloss; a war-season camp at the northern reach of Shoshone raiding, dated only by the narrator’s age (kept off the division track, which would otherwise put the Shoshone north of every Blackfoot division)
source: David Thompson’s Narrative of His Explorations in Western America, 1784–1812, ed. Tyrrell (Champlain Society, 1916), pp. 328–29

source_says: “Around 1734 the Omaha established their first village west of the Missouri River on Bow Creek in present-day Cedar County, Nebraska”
source: Wikipedia, “Omaha people” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Biesterfeldt site on the Sheyenne River near Lisbon, North Dakota: “an independent group of Cheyennes is believed to have occupied it c. 1724–1780”
source: Wikipedia, “Biesterfeldt Site” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: 1736: 300 Sioux men east of the Mississippi and 2,000 on the prairies
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 722

source_says: M.H. Wright: about 8,000 in 1736
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Opler, “Lipan Apache”, p. 945

source_says: La Vérendrye, from Fort La Reine (Oct. 1738): “Joining a large band of Assiniboines, he pushed southwest across the prairie” to the Mandan
source: Wikipedia, “Pierre Gaultier de Varennes, sieur de La Vérendrye” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: The Mallet brothers visit the Panimaha (Skiri) at the mouth of the Loup, 1739
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, p. 518

source_says: 1739 or 1740: the French build Fort de Cavagnial next to the Kansa village, then near the mouth of Salt Creek
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Bailey and Young, “Kansa”, p. 463

source_says: “An Arikara village, near where present-day Pierre, South Dakota developed, was visited in 1743 by two sons of… La Vérendrye”
source: Wikipedia, “Arikara” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Mille Lacs, before the Ojibwe destroyed Kathio “in about the year 1750” and expelled the Dakota (a battle there is recorded in 1745)
source: Wikipedia, “Battle of Kathio” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: After abandoning Mille Lacs in the mid-18th century the Mdewakanton settle on the Rum River, and a few years later move their villages to the Mississippi and lower Minnesota (date ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 727

source_says: 1748–49: French deserters pass two Wichita villages a mile and a half apart on the west side of the Arkansas (Deer Creek and Bryson-Paddock), population 1,500–2,500, mostly Taovaya (a partial count)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Newcomb, “Wichita”, p. 550

source_says: “Numbering between ten and fifteen thousand at midcentury”
source: Hämäläinen, The Comanche Empire (2008)

source_says: Fort de Cavagnial (1744–64), on the bluffs above Salt Creek north of Fort Leavenworth, “roughly in the same location as a major Kansa village”
source: Wikipedia, “Fort de Cavagnial” (site coordinates and participants); Wikipedia, “Kaw people” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Clark, 20 Oct. 1804: old fortified Mandan villages below the Heart River; the Arikara chief “tels me that nation lived in a number villages on each side of the river and the Troubleson Seauex caused them to move about 40 miles higher up”
source: Lewis & Clark journals, ed. Moulton (UNL online edition), entries for 19–20 Oct. 1804

source_says: “The Mandan population in 1750 seems to have been about 9,000”
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Wood and Irwin, “Mandan”, p. 351

source_says: Utz site: “occupied by the Missouri tribe from c. 15th to the late 18th centuries… probably their principal village area during their first contact with Europeans”
source: Wikipedia, “Utz Site” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Deer Creek and Bryson-Paddock: “18th century fortified villages of the Wichita… along the Arkansas River in Kay County”
source: Wikipedia, “Deer Creek/Bryson Paddock Sites” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: 1752: seeking better trade, the Kansa move their village to the Kansas River near its confluence with the Missouri
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Bailey and Young, “Kansa”, p. 464

source_says: Louisiana governor, 1754: about 950 warriors (Din and Nasatir)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Bailey, “Osage”, p. 492

source_says: Henday meets “Asinepoets” (“thought by some to be Assiniboines”) on 20 Sept. 1754, nine days after crossing into present Alberta near Chauvin
source: Wikipedia, “Anthony Henday” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Henday reaches “a massive Archithinues (Blackfoot) encampment” of 322 tipis, “thought to have been located a few miles west of Pine Lake, near present-day Innisfail”, 14 Oct. 1754 (which Blackfoot division is not said; placed with the Siksika, the northernmost)
source: Wikipedia, “Anthony Henday” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: “The earliest known contact of Gros Ventre with whites was around 1754, between the north and south forks of the Saskatchewan River”
source: Wikipedia, “Gros Ventre” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: An “old” Iowa village on the site of Council Bluffs, seen by Lewis and Clark; occupied within reach of Fort de Cavagnial (1744); date ours, before the move east about 1765
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Wedel, “Iowa”, p. 434

source_says: “Situated east of the Crows, the Kiowa took possession of the Black Hills… They continued to occupy the Black Hills until about the close of the last century”; the Apache part of their camp circle
source: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), p. 156

source_says: “Situated east of the Crows, the Kiowa took possession of the Black Hills… They continued to occupy the Black Hills until about the close of the last century”; the Apache part of their camp circle
source: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), p. 156

source_says: Henday, with his Cree guide Attickasish and Cree companions, reaches the North Saskatchewan near the mouth of the Sturgeon River, 3 Mar. 1755, and camps while canoes are built; “more fur-laden Indians arrived”; leaves 27 Apr.
source: Wikipedia, “Anthony Henday” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: By 1757 the Taovaya have moved to the Red River just west of the Western Cross Timbers: a fortified village on the north bank (Longest site), an Iscani village downstream
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Newcomb, “Wichita”, p. 550

source_says: Lipan gather at Mission Santa Cruz de San Sabá, 1757
source: Wikipedia, “Mission Santa Cruz de San Sabá” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Kerlerec: 150 Missouria men
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Schweitzer, “Otoe and Missouria”, p. 453, table 1, citing Kerlerec

source_says: Kerlerec: 800 men
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Liberty, Wood, and Irwin, “Omaha”, p. 415, table 2, citing Kerlerec

source_says: Kerlerec: 100 Otoe men
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Schweitzer, “Otoe and Missouria”, p. 453, table 1, citing Kerlerec

source_says: Kerlerec: the Panimaha, on the Platte 25 leagues from its mouth, number 600 men bearing arms
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, pp. 518, 563

source_says: Mission Santa Cruz de San Sabá near present Menard attacked by “a force of some 2,000 Comanches and allied tribes”, March 1758 (a war expedition, kept off the division track)
source: Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online, “Comanche Indians”

source_says: Parrilla’s attack on the Taovaya twin villages on the Red River, Oct. 1759
source: Wikipedia, “Battle of the Twin Villages” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: At separation from the Sioux (traditional date c. 1760) “at least 1,500 lodges, averaging six souls to a lodge”; then about the head of the Minnesota & Des Moines, Devils Lake, Lac qui Parle
source: Denig, “Indian Tribes of the Upper Missouri” (ms. c. 1854; BAE 46th Annual Report, 1930); Hodge’s editor notes the date is far too late

source_says: Big Hidatsa village, “occupied between ca. 1740 and 1850”, Knife River
source: Wikipedia, “Big Hidatsa Village Site” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: An estimate of 1760: 1,100 souls
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: “About 1760 they moved east and came to live along the Mississippi between the Iowa and Des Moines Rivers”
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: Mid-18th century: Yanktonai territory from Big Stone Lake and Lake Traverse west to the Missouri (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 731

source_says: Mid-18th century: Yanktonai territory from Big Stone Lake and Lake Traverse west to the Missouri (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 731

source_says: Mid-18th century: Yankton territory the lower Big Sioux and the heads of the Floyd, Little Sioux and Des Moines (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 731

source_says: 1762: the two leaders at the El Cañón missions had 700 followers, and ten other local groups were known: “between 3,000 and 4,000 Lipans living in central Texas” (Tunnell and Newcomb)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Opler, “Lipan Apache”, p. 942

source_says: Lipan at the El Cañón missions on the upper Nueces, 1762–71
source: Mission San Lorenzo de la Santa Cruz (El Cañón) (recalled; not checked against the text this round)

source_says: Biesterfeldt site, occupied c. 1724–1780
source: Wikipedia, “Biesterfeldt Site” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: From the 1760s to 1851 the Mdewakanton villages stand on the Mississippi and the lower Minnesota (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, pp. 727–29

source_says: 1760s: the Wahpekute villages on the Cannon River and at Traverse des Sioux (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 729

source_says: 1760s: the Wahpeton villages on the Minnesota, above the Mdewakanton (a range; centre ours)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 727

source_says: William Pink reports a small group of Assiniboines in the Prince Albert area with many horses; they had given up canoes (a single group; kept off the division track)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie and Miller, “Assiniboine”, p. 574

source_says: 1765 and the years following: the Iowa move east near the mouth of the Des Moines (On the Des Moines River, 1765–1837)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Wedel, “Iowa”, p. 435

source_says: “In 1770 when French traders opened relations with them they were a little below Cheyenne River”
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: Truteau’s pre-epidemic 4,000 warriors (Parks: about 16,000, at least 10,000): 16,000
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Arikara”, p. 387, table 3, citing Truteau’s pre-epidemic 4,000 warriors (Parks: about 16,000, at least 10,000)

source_says: 1772: the Wichita and Tawehash “seem to have had about 600 warriors”
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 306

source_says: Tawakoni: 36 houses and 120 warriors in the Trinity village, 30 families in the Brazos village (Mézières)
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 303

source_says: Cocking travels inland with Pegogamaw Cree, “who met their families at the well-known rendezvous at present James Smith First Nation”, summer 1772 (the Pegogamaw a band of the Saskatchewan Cree, filed with the Fort des Prairies division; a band, kept off the division track)
source: Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan, “Cocking, Matthew (1743–99)”; DCB, “Cocking, Matthew”

source_says: From the rendezvous the Pegogamaw make a circuit west to the Eagle Hills and the Thickwood Hills, “hunting out on the open plains southwest of modern Biggar”, autumn–winter 1772–73
source: Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan, “Cocking, Matthew (1743–99)”; DCB, “Cocking, Matthew”

source_says: Early December 1772: Cocking meets 28 tepees of Gros Ventre at a buffalo pound near the Eagle Hills; they have already split into winter bands (a band; kept off the division track)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Fowler and Flannery, “Gros Ventre”, p. 678

source_says: Gaignard learned the Comanches “comprise fully four thousand warriors”; Hämäläinen derives about 16,000
source: Gaignard (1773–74) via Hämäläinen, The Comanche Empire

source_says: The circuit ends at a bison pound near Red Deer Hill, south of Prince Albert, spring 1773
source: Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan, “Cocking, Matthew (1743–99)”; DCB, “Cocking, Matthew”

source_says: “Around 1775 the Omaha developed a new village, probably located near present-day Homer, Nebraska” (Big Village)
source: Wikipedia, “Omaha people” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Winter 1774–75: Peter Pond travels nine days up the Minnesota to a camp of Sioux he calls Yankton (“probably Yanktonai”), some 200 miles above his post (a camp; kept off the division track)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), DeMallie, “Sioux Until 1850”, p. 731

source_says: Cruzat, 1777: 250 warriors
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)

source_says: Houck: 200 Missouria warriors
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Schweitzer, “Otoe and Missouria”, p. 453, table 1, citing Houck

source_says: Houck: 100 Otoe warriors
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Schweitzer, “Otoe and Missouria”, p. 453, table 1, citing Houck

source_says: Cruzat, Nov. 1777: the Chawi on the west bank of Skull Creek below the Platte (Barcal site)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, p. 518

source_says: Cruzat, 1777: the Kitkahahki in a village on the Republican River
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, p. 518

source_says: 1777: about 300 Panimahas leave the Skiri on the Loup for the Red River, joining the Taovaya; they stay into the 19th century (part; kept off the division track)
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Parks, “Pawnee”, p. 518

source_says: Lehmer: villages reduced between 1750 and 1780, population about 4,400 before the epidemic
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Wood and Irwin, “Mandan”, p. 351

source_says: “In 1778, the Taovaya village at Spanish Fort had 123 houses and across the Red River a Wichita town had another 37 houses”
source: Wikipedia, “Taovaya” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: Tawehash (Taovaya): two villages of 160 lodges, “800 fighting men and youths”
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 303

source_says: Tawakoni: the two towns, then on the Brazos, held “more than 300 warriors” (Mézières, 1778–79)
source: Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 303

source_says: Voget: “a population between 8,000 and 10,000 before the smallpox epidemics of 1781”
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Voget, “Crow”, p. 714

source_says: Clark, 22 Oct. 1804: “the upper of the 6 Villages the Mandans occupied about 25 years ago… entirely cut off by the Sioux”
source: Lewis & Clark journals, ed. Moulton (UNL online edition), entry for 22 Oct. 1804

source_says: April 1779, De Mézières at the Spanish Fort villages: 37 grass lodges on the north bank (Wichita proper) and 123 in the Taovaya village on the south bank, “more than 800 men and youths”
source: DeMallie, ed., Handbook of North American Indians, vol. 13: Plains (2001), Newcomb, “Wichita”, p. 551

source_says: Anza defeats Cuerno Verde (“likely of the Kotsoteka”) near the Greenhorn Mountains, 3 Sept. 1779
source: Wikipedia, “Cuerno Verde” (site coordinates and participants)

source_says: 3,000 Arapaho in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 386

source_says: About 3,000 Arikara in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 274

source_says: 10,000 Assiniboin in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 388

source_says: “25,000 Dakota of all divisions, exclusive of the Assiniboin” in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952), p. 283

source_says: Cheyenne and Sutaio 3,500 in 1780
source: Mooney, “The Aboriginal Population of America North of Mexico” (1928), as given by Swanton, The Indian Tribes of North America (BAE Bulletin 145, 1952)
